newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Defiant Argentine police threaten to strike.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Argentine police threaten to strike.

text.p: Thousands of Argentine policemen on Saturday demanded better pay and working conditions and threatened a strike, just 24 hours after being told to rid the force of corruption or face mass dismissals.

Nearly 5,000 non-commisioned officers of the Buenos Aires province police force, by far the largest in the country, met at an undisclosed site and issued a nine-point document with their demands, their spokesman told the private DyN news agency.
The document, signed by representatives of the province's 18 regional units, said they would go on an unlimited strike on March 24 unless their wage and other demands were met.

"This pursues no political ends, neither does it seek to disrupt the country's democratic system," said the document, entitled "Communique Number One" -- the same term the military used in the past to advise citizens a coup had taken place and their constitutional rights had been scrapped.

The move came the day after Buenos Aires Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, a 1999 presidential hopeful, summoned 1,000 top officers and warned he was putting all 48,000 provincial agents on "dispensable" status, meaning they could be fired.

Duhalde's threat was preceded by a series of probes showing corruption in the provincial force and opinion polls revealing popular fear of the police -- a scenario analysts say could thwart his presidential ambitions.
"When people see a squad car at night, rather than feeling protected, they feel fear," said Duhalde, second in the hierarchy of the ruling Peronist Party.

Both him and President Carlos Menem have been pictured holding posters of news photographer Jose Luis Cabezas, whose death-squad style murder in January triggered a wave of indignation and calls for an all-out war against corruption.

"We don't forget Mr. Cabezas," said the police in the document. "But we don't forget either the 68 comrades who have fallen" in the line of duty in the past three years, they said, demanding better health care, faster promotions, and popular recognition.

Officers have been caught trafficking drugs, four have been indicted for involvement in a 1994 bomb attack on a Jewish centre that killed 86 people and there has been case after case of police brutality ranging from beatings to youngsters killed by trigger-happy officers.
